description: We are a passionate software development team bridging the gap between complex space engineering and youth education. Combining expertise in programming, interactive design, and systems logic, we are building tools that make real-world mission trade-offs both tangible and fun.
summary: Welcome to Sols of Survival! For this NASA Space Apps challenge, we wanted more than a building game, so we made a survival adventure where every storm is real. Meet Nova, Cosmo, Rocket and Luna, four Space Kittens sent to run a tiny base on Mars. Their mission sounds simple: keep the crew alive for five Sols (a Sol is one day on Mars). But the Sun has other plans. Along the way, the crew faces events that really happened, like the giant sunspot of 2014, the 2017 solar storm that doubled radiation on Mars, the 2018 dust storm that silenced NASA's Opportunity rover, and the record-breaking storm of May 2024 measured by Curiosity. And this isn't just a story, it's you in charge. As the player, you pack the rocket, build the base and jump into hands-on missions like cleaning solar panels, melting ice for water and stacking bricks against radiation. Every choice helps one thing and costs another, just like it does for real mission planners. This is NASA space weather data like kids have never seen it before: not in charts or reports, but as a base they have to protect.
details:
Nah, We'd Win’s Project Solution

Sols of Survival is an educational survival game that teaches kids aged 7 to 12 what it really takes to keep a crew alive on Mars or the Moon, by turning real NASA space weather data into a story-driven base-building game. Players team up with a Space Kitten, build their own outpost, and use hands-on mini games to protect their crew from real solar storms, making space science both fun and easy to understand.

How Does Our Solution Work

In the game, four Space Kittens, Nova, Cosmo, Rocket and Luna, are sent to run a small base on Mars. The player picks one as their partner, packs a rocket with only 7 crates out of 11, and builds a base with Power Stations, Greenhouses, Water Stations, Radiation Shields and a Research Lab. Then they have to keep three bars above zero: Power, Life Support and Crew Health. Every Sol (one day on Mars), the base faces a space weather event that really happened, and the player spends 2 actions on hands-on missions before deciding how to face it.

  • A Calm Day (Mars, Sol 1):
    The crew lands on a quiet day, and the kitten shows the player around the base. But even calm days aren’t safe on Mars. NASA’s Curiosity rover measured about 0.67 millisieverts of radiation per day on the surface, so the crew’s health slowly drops every Sol. The player uses this day to build up their base before the storms arrive.
  • The Giant Sunspot (October 2014):
    Sunspot AR 2192, the biggest of its solar cycle, fires an X3.1 flare on 24 October 2014. It looks scary, but no cloud of particles comes toward the planet. Players who hide in the shelter lose a whole day of work for nothing, while players who did the Watch the Sun mission in the Research Lab already know the storm won’t follow. Through this, players learn that forecasting the Sun is hard and that good data changes everything.
  • The Storm That Reached the Ground (September 2017):
    On 10 September 2017, an X8.2 flare sends a particle storm across the solar system, and Curiosity measures radiation on the Martian surface at more than double anything it had seen before. In the gameplay, players protect the crew by choosing:
    Choice 1: Hide in the Radiation Shield bunker, which blocks most of the radiation but stops all work.
    Choice 2: Use a saved action to reinforce the walls.
    Choice 3: Keep working and take the risk.
    Players can also press Ask Earth, but Mars was on the far side of the Sun that day, so the reply takes 40 minutes and arrives after the storm hits. Through this, players learn why real crews on Mars have to make their own decisions.
  • The Dust Storm That Ended Opportunity (June 2018):
    A dust storm grows until it covers the whole planet, and sunlight drops so low that solar panels barely work. This is the same storm that silenced NASA’s Opportunity rover, which sent its last message on 10 June 2018. In the gameplay, players save their base by:
    Task 1: Rubbing the dust off the solar panels in the Dust Off the Panels mini game.
    Task 2: Connecting the right wires to charge the battery before the storm.
    Task 3: Deciding whether to power down the greenhouse or keep everything running.
    Through this, players discover that energy on Mars depends on the environment.
  • The Strongest Storm Ever Measured on Mars (May 2024):
    The final test. On 20 May 2024, a flare estimated at X12 sends the biggest burst of radiation Curiosity has ever recorded, 8,100 micrograys, which is about the same as 30 chest X-rays for an astronaut standing next to the rover. Everything the player built is tested at once: shields, shelter and stored power.
  • The Moon Base (Lunar Night and August 1972):
    Players can also choose the Moon’s south pole instead. There they face the lunar night, about 14 Earth days without sunlight, and the August 1972 solar storm that hit between the Apollo 16 and Apollo 17 missions. On the Moon, Earth answers in about a second, which shows kids how much distance changes everything.
  • Today’s Space Weather (Live NASA Data):
    In this mode, the game asks NASA’s DONKI database about the last 7 days of real solar activity and turns it into 3 Sols. If NASA can’t be reached, the game clearly switches to stored events and marks them OFFLINE, so stored data is never shown as live.

Every station also has 2 hands-on missions, and each one comes with a real science fact, from planting and harvesting crops (ISS astronauts first ate space-grown lettuce in 2015) to melting ice (Phoenix found ice on Mars in 2008), recycling water (the ISS recycles about 98% of its water) and stacking regolith bricks against radiation.

When the crew makes it through all five Sols, the kitten celebrates with a Certificate of Survival and a chart of everything that happened. If the crew doesn’t make it, there’s no “Game Over”. The kitten explains what went wrong and what to try next!

The game benefits

kids, students, teachers and families by:

  • Teaching how space weather, radiation and energy affect life on Mars and the Moon.
  • Showing that every engineering choice has a cost, using real events from NASA’s records.
  • Turning NASA’s open data into something kids can see, play and remember, instead of charts and reports.
  • Giving teachers a Family/Class mode with discussion questions and a printable debrief.

Our goal

To make NASA’s space weather data accessible and exciting for young kids, and to help them understand what real crews will face when they live on Mars and the Moon. Our game is a prototype, so bar sizes and station outputs are simplified to keep it playable, and the game says so on its “Real vs. Simplified” screen. We focused on solar storms, radiation and dust storms, and our game doesn’t yet cover other challenges like the long-term effects of space on the human body, which we’d like to add next using NASA’s space biology data.

Tools and Technologies Used

Coding Languages:

  • JavaScript, HTML and CSS → for the whole game, which runs in any browser with no account.
  • Web Audio API → for all the music and sound effects, made in code.

Data Sources:

  • NASA DONKI → for the real dates and strengths of our solar flares and particle storms, and for live space weather from the last 7 days.
  • NASA Open APIs → for the live DONKI connection, the Astronomy Picture of the Day on the title screen, and real Curiosity photos.
  • Curiosity RAD measurements and NASA mission news → for the real radiation numbers and the story behind each event.

Use of AI:

Manus AI
How it was used: Used to structure the core game logic, state flow, and turn-by-turn resource trade-off mechanics. All scientific rules and numbers were verified by our team.
Claude (Anthropic)
How it was used: Used for writing and refactoring front-end HTML/CSS/JavaScript code and fixing gameplay bugs.
Google Flow (Google Labs)
How it was used: Used to generate initial 2D illustration drafts for our Space Kitten characters, isometric habitat buildings, station interiors, and event cards, which were then cropped, cleaned, and color-matched by the team.
